definition: Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortisation. A proxy for operating cash flow, calculated as operating income plus D&A. Used to compare profitability across capital structures.
Cash generated by operations minus capital expenditures. Represents cash available to pay down debt, return to shareholders, or invest. FCF = Operating Cash Flow - Capex.
Revenue minus cost of goods sold, divided by revenue. Expressed as a percentage, it measures how efficiently a company produces its goods or services before operating expenses.
Operating income divided by revenue. Measures profitability from core operations before interest and taxes. Also called EBIT margin.
Net income divided by revenue. The bottom-line profitability measure showing what percentage of revenue remains as profit after all expenses, taxes, and interest.
Price-to-Earnings ratio. Share price divided by earnings per share (EPS). Indicates how much investors pay per dollar of earnings. High P/E may signal growth expectations or overvaluation.
Enterprise Value divided by EBITDA. A capital-structure-neutral valuation multiple. Commonly used in M&A to compare companies with different leverage levels. Lower values may indicate undervaluation.
Total debt divided by shareholders' equity. Measures financial leverage. A high ratio means more debt financing relative to equity, implying higher financial risk.
Current assets divided by current liabilities. Measures short-term liquidity. A ratio above 1 indicates the company can cover its near-term obligations with current assets.
Current assets minus inventory, divided by current liabilities. A stricter liquidity test than the current ratio, excluding inventory which may not be quickly converted to cash.
Compound Annual Growth Rate. The steady annual growth rate that would take an investment from its beginning to ending value over a given period. CAGR = (End/Start)^(1/n) - 1.
Discounted Cash Flow. A valuation method that estimates the present value of future cash flows by discounting them at a rate reflecting the time value of money and risk (usually WACC).
Weighted Average Cost of Capital. The blended cost of equity and debt financing, weighted by their proportions in the capital structure. Used as the discount rate in DCF analysis.
A measure of a stock's volatility relative to the overall market. A beta of 1 moves with the market; above 1 is more volatile; below 1 is less volatile. Used in CAPM to estimate cost of equity.
Net income divided by shareholders' equity. Measures how efficiently management uses equity capital to generate profit. Also known as ROE.
Net income divided by total assets. Measures how efficiently a company uses its asset base to generate earnings. Also known as ROA.
Cash received for goods or services not yet delivered. Recorded as a liability on the balance sheet. Common in subscription businesses. Recognised as revenue when the obligation is fulfilled.
Money owed to a company by customers for goods or services already delivered but not yet paid. A current asset on the balance sheet. High AR relative to revenue may indicate collection issues.

An intangible asset recorded when a company is acquired for more than the fair value of its net identifiable assets. Reflects brand value, customer relationships, and synergies. Subject to annual impairment testing.

Current assets minus current liabilities. Measures short-term operational liquidity. Positive working capital means a company can fund its day-to-day operations. Also = Accounts Receivable + Inventory - Accounts Payable.
Capital Expenditure. Funds spent on acquiring, upgrading, or maintaining long-term physical assets such as property, plant, and equipment. Deducted from operating cash flow to derive free cash flow.
The systematic allocation of the cost of a tangible asset over its useful life. A non-cash expense on the income statement that reduces book value of assets. Added back in cash flow statements.
The gradual write-off of an intangible asset (e.g., patents, trademarks, acquired customer lists) over its useful life. Analogous to depreciation for tangible assets. Both are added back in EBITDA.

An annualised revenue estimate based on current-period performance. Calculated as most recent quarterly revenue multiplied by 4. Used for fast-growing companies where historical annual figures are less representative.
The rate at which a company spends its cash reserves. Monthly gross burn is total cash outflows; net burn subtracts revenue. Dividing cash balance by net burn gives runway in months.
Average number of days to collect payment after a sale. DSO = (Accounts Receivable / Revenue) × Number of Days. Lower DSO indicates faster collections and better cash flow management.
Cost of Goods Sold divided by average inventory. Measures how quickly inventory is sold and replaced. Higher turnover indicates efficient inventory management; low turnover may signal obsolescence.

Revenue divided by average total assets. Measures how efficiently a company uses its assets to generate sales. Part of the DuPont decomposition of ROE: ROE = Net Margin × Asset Turnover × Equity Multiplier.
EBIT divided by interest expense. Measures how easily a company can pay interest on outstanding debt. A ratio below 1.5 is generally considered a warning sign of financial distress.
Share price divided by book value per share. Compares market valuation to accounting net asset value. A ratio below 1 may indicate the market values the company at less than its net assets.
